content: Epilepsy is a prevalent neurological disorder, affecting approximately 1% of the population. Among individuals with epilepsy, nearly 30% exhibit resistance to currently available antiepileptic drugs (AEDs), necessitating the use of multiple AEDs in combination. Tiagabine is a newer AED that can be employed as an adjunctive (add-on) therapy alongside standard AEDs. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and tolerability of tiagabine as an add-on treatment for individuals with drug-resistant focal seizures. This review is an update of a Cochrane review last published in 2014. For the latest update, databases such as the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web), MEDLINE, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform were searched on January 22, 2019. No language restrictions were applied. Additionally, the manufacturers of tiagabine and field experts were contacted to identify ongoing or unpublished studies. The review included randomized, placebo-controlled add-on trials involving individuals of any age with focal epilepsy. Eligible studies could be double-blind, single-blind, or unblinded, with either parallel or cross-over designs, and required a minimum treatment duration of eight weeks. Trials with active drug control groups were also included. Two independent reviewers assessed the trials for inclusion and extracted data following Cochrane Collaboration's standard methodological procedures. Disagreements were resolved through discussion. The outcomes evaluated included a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency, treatment withdrawal, adverse effects, and impacts on cognition and quality of life. Primary analyses were conducted on an intention-to-treat basis, and worst-case and best-case analyses were calculated for seizure outcomes. Dose-response relationships were analyzed using regression models. The risk of bias in each study was assessed using the Cochrane 'Risk of bias' tool. No new studies were added since the previous update in 2014. The review included six trials (four parallel-group and two cross-over trials) with a total of 948 participants. For the primary comparison of tiagabine versus placebo, participants ranged in age from 12 to 77 years, and treatment periods lasted between 12 and 22 weeks. The overall risk ratio (RR) for achieving a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency with tiagabine compared to placebo was 3.16 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.97 to 5.07; 3 trials; 769 participants; high-certainty evidence). However, due to variability in response rates across trials, regression models could not reliably estimate responses to individual doses. The risk ratio for treatment withdrawal with tiagabine compared to placebo was 1.81 (95% CI 1.25 to 2.62; 3 trials; 769 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Dizziness and tremor were significantly associated with tiagabine therapy. Limited data on cognitive and quality-of-life outcomes suggested no significant effects on cognition, mood, or adjustment. One trial compared tiagabine with an active drug control (topiramate) and found no significant differences between the two drugs in achieving a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.19 to 1.58; 1 trial; 41 participants) or in treatment withdrawal (RR 1.43, 95% CI 0.74 to 2.74; 1 trial; 41 participants). Of the six included studies, two were judged to have a low risk of bias, three had an unclear risk of bias, and one had a high risk of bias. The least reported trial design factor was the method of randomization sequence generation, which raised the most concerns regarding bias. The overall certainty of the evidence was rated as moderate to high using the GRADE approach, although the evidence for some adverse effects, such as nausea and tremor, was rated as low certainty. In conclusion, tiagabine was found to reduce seizure frequency but was associated with certain adverse effects when used as an add-on treatment for individuals with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. The findings are primarily applicable to adults and adolescents, as none of the included trials involved participants under the age of 12. No significant differences were observed between tiagabine and topiramate as add-on therapies; however, this conclusion is based on limited evidence from a single trial.
